newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BSkyB's Chisholm backs new boss for new era.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BSkyB's Chisholm backs new boss for new era.

text.p: BSkyB Plc chief executive Sam Chisholm gave a ringing endorsement to his successor on Friday while the company said the move into digital television would put a brake on profit growth.

The dominant force in British pay TV, BSkyB reported a 22 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 314 million pounds ($499 million) in the year to June 30. The figures marked the end of an era for feisty New Zealander Chisholm, who is stepping down on health grounds in December.

BSkyB shares, under pressure since Chisholm's departure was announced, fell 34.5p to 435.5p. Analysts said the profit figure fell a little short of expectations when one-off items were stripped out and cited uncertainties over the cost of going digital.

Chisholm gave his backing to his successor, American Mark Booth. Booth is moving from JSkyB, Rupert Murdoch's Japanese satellite TV venture, to BSkyB where Murdoch's News Corp is also the largest shareholder.
"He's absolutely the right man to take this company forward," Chisholm said, describing Booth, who has 17 years experience in pay TV around the world, as "quite a little wizard at what he does".
Booth's challenge is to lead BSkyB into the multi-channel digital age.

He has a tough act to follow as Chisholm, described by Murdoch as "one of the best executives I have ever worked with" has turned BSkyB into one of the corporate success stories of the 1990s. The company now boasts 5.9 million UK subscribers -- one in four of all households.
BSkyB has created huge competition for the four established terrestrial channels and its partnership with English soccer's premier league has breathed fresh life into the national game.
BSkyB confirmed it was on course to launch 200-channel digital services in Britain in spring 1998 and said that the associated costs effectively ruled out large growth in operating profit this year.
"BSkyB endorses the market view that operating profits are likely to be maintained," finance director Richard Brooke told Reuters. Operating profit rose 19 percent to 374 million pounds in 1996/97.

The digital service will feature near video on demand films, showing a movie on a pay per view basis with staggered start times throughout an evening. BSkyB is in talks with Hollywood studios on pay per view rights.

BSkyB has teamed up with British Telecom, Midland Bank and Japan's Matsushita to set up the British Interactive Broadcasting (BIB) venture to provide online services such as home shopping and banking for digital satellite customers. These will be launched a few months after the TV channels go on air.

A BIB subsidy will bring the retail cost of digital set-top boxes or decoders under 200 pounds. A decoder is required to view the new services, which BSkyB aims to deliver to homes via both satellite dishes and cable.
BSkyB believes the subsidy will mean a more rapid take-up of digital services in Britain than in other countries such as Germany and Italy.
"At this company we do sit back, think it through and get it right...We think we have got it right," said Chisholm, who will remain a BSkyB consultant and board member. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
